questions.question: At about 70 km/h, how far to each side does the average driver's peripheral vision reach?
options: About 30 degrees
About 90 degrees
About 60 degrees
About 120 degrees
questions.explanation: The field of view narrows further as speed rises, so a faster driver takes in less of what is happening at the roadside.

questions.question: On a carriageway with two lanes running in the same direction, which lane should you normally use?
options: The right-hand lane
The left-hand lane
Whichever lane is emptier
Either lane, if you keep to the limit
questions.explanation: The left lane is kept free for overtaking, for preparing a left turn, and for evening out heavy traffic loads.

questions.question: What does the term speed blindness describe?
options: Being dazzled by oncoming headlights at high speed
Failing to notice the speed limit signs along a route
Losing peripheral vision when driving very fast
Losing your sense of how fast you are actually driving
questions.explanation: It creeps in after a long stretch on a good, quiet road and becomes dangerous when conditions worsen, for example where asphalt turns into gravel.

questions.question: While you are driving, what is the only way to reduce your vehicle's kinetic energy?
options: Reduce the load the vehicle is carrying
Change down into a lower gear
Increase the gap to the vehicle ahead
Reduce the speed of the vehicle
questions.explanation: Many accidents happen because drivers underestimate this energy, and once you are on the move only lower speed brings it down.

questions.question: Under the traffic law, what does the posted maximum speed limit actually mean?
options: The speed drivers are expected to keep on that road
The highest speed allowed when conditions are at their best
The safest speed for an ordinary car in rain
The highest speed allowed whatever the conditions
questions.explanation: The driver must judge each situation and adjust to the road surface, traffic, visibility, weather and the vehicle, often driving well below the sign.

questions.question: What is the maximum speed limit on gravel roads outside urban areas?
options: 60 km/h
70 km/h
80 km/h
90 km/h
questions.explanation: Asphalt roads outside urban areas allow 90 km/h; the lower gravel figure reflects the reduced grip of a loose surface.

questions.question: A car towing an unregistered trailer may not be driven faster than what speed?
options: 70 km/h
60 km/h
80 km/h
90 km/h
questions.explanation: A registered trailer or comparable object allows up to 80 km/h, but an unregistered one is held to the lower figure.

questions.question: What is the highest speed limit that can be posted anywhere in Iceland?
options: 90 km/h
80 km/h
100 km/h
110 km/h
questions.explanation: Iceland has no freeways, so its limits never reach the levels found on motorways abroad.

questions.question: You have entered a bend too fast and feel the centrifugal force building. What is the safest response?
options: Brake hard to scrub off the excess speed
Steer sharply towards the inside of the bend
Stay calm and ease off the accelerator
Accelerate to pull the car through the bend
questions.explanation: Stamping on the brakes can stop the wheels rolling; letting them keep turning preserves grip and steering control through the bend.

questions.question: What is meant by a blind summit?
options: A crest where drivers on each side cannot see one another
A hill so steep that heavy vehicles have to stop
A crest where overtaking is allowed only downhill
A bend at the top of a hill without road markings
questions.explanation: An oncoming vehicle can appear without warning, and low crests or crests inside a bend are especially deceptive because the danger looks smaller than it is.

questions.question: Having stopped for a pedestrian crossing, how far back from it should your car normally be?
options: At least 10 metres, about two to three car lengths
At least 3 metres, about half a car length
At least 5 metres, about one car length
At least 20 metres, about five car lengths
questions.explanation: The gap gives a following driver who tries to overtake time and room to see the crossing; only in heavy slow traffic may it shrink, and never below about one car length.

questions.question: When may you overtake another vehicle just before or on a pedestrian crossing?
options: Only when no pedestrian is in sight
Only where the crossing has no traffic lights
Never, whether or not pedestrians are nearby
Only when traffic is heavy and moving slowly
questions.explanation: Changing lanes or overtaking there is strictly forbidden, because the overtaken vehicle hides pedestrians from the driver coming past.

questions.question: A pedestrian at the roadside is carrying a white cane. What does this tell you?
options: The person is elderly and moves slowly
The person is blind
The person has difficulty hearing traffic
The person has reduced mobility
questions.explanation: Drive slowly and leave plenty of room, since a startled pedestrian in this group may react in a way you cannot foresee.

questions.question: When is the risk of meeting loose horses on the road at its greatest?
options: On bright summer evenings
During the spring lambing season
In the darkness of autumn and winter
On calm mornings in early summer
questions.explanation: Spring is the dangerous season for lambs rather than horses; loose horses are hardest to spot in the long darkness of autumn and winter.

questions.question: You reach the scene of a traffic accident and your assistance is clearly not needed. What should you do?
options: Stop and wait until the police have arrived
Park nearby and offer to help anyway
Keep your normal speed to clear the area
Drive slowly past without stopping
questions.explanation: Slowing down is required for safety, but stopping when you are not needed only obstructs traffic and the emergency vehicles.

questions.question: In the sense used by the traffic law, when are you stopping the vehicle?
options: When you halt because the traffic ahead has stopped
When you halt so that a passenger can get in or out
When you halt because a police officer orders it
When you halt for longer than unloading requires
questions.explanation: Halting for traffic conditions or on police orders is not stopping in the legal sense, and halting longer than the errand needs counts as parking instead.

questions.question: Where a road has no marked parking spaces, on which side must you leave the car?
options: On the side with the wider verge
On the side facing oncoming traffic
On the left side of the road
On the right side of the road
questions.explanation: Parking on the left is recommended only in certain one-way streets in urban areas; elsewhere the right side is the rule.

questions.question: May a driver who is not disabled halt briefly in a parking space reserved for disabled persons?
options: Yes, provided the vehicle is not left unattended
Yes, for as long as loading or unloading takes
Yes, outside the business hours of the parking meter
No, neither stopping nor parking is allowed there
questions.explanation: The restriction covers stopping as well as parking, so even a short halt in such a space is prohibited.

questions.question: How close to a bus stop may a vehicle be stopped or parked?
options: No closer than 5 metres
No closer than 15 metres
No closer than 10 metres
No closer than 25 metres
questions.explanation: Both stopping and parking are banned inside that distance so that buses can pull in to the kerb and passengers can board safely.

questions.question: What must you do with the car before you walk away from a parking space?
options: Lock it and take the keys away with you
Leave it unlocked in case it has to be moved
Leave the keys hidden somewhere inside it
Lock it but leave a window slightly open
questions.explanation: It is prohibited to leave a vehicle in a condition where a stranger could easily drive it off, and visible valuables should not be left behind either.

questions.question: Which loose-sheep situation does the book single out as the most dangerous?
options: A ewe on one side of the road and her lamb on the other
A single ram standing still in the middle of the road
A flock grazing behind a fence beside the road
Sheep following a farm vehicle along the verge
questions.explanation: Sheep running loose can cross suddenly at any time, which applies particularly to young lambs in springtime; the book names a ewe and her offspring separated by the road as the most dangerous case of all.

questions.question: If you accidentally hit a farm animal on the road, what must you do?
options: Try to contact the animal's owner
Continue on your way if the animal runs off
Wait at the scene only if another vehicle is damaged
Leave a note only if the animal is visibly injured
questions.explanation: The duty to try to reach the owner applies regardless of whether the animal appears hurt or bolts away afterward.
